## Goal

This notebook does for case study 2 (Figure 3 and Supplementary Figure S1 of the paper) what notebook 01 did for case
study 1. The files were downloaded by `scripts/case2/download_case2.sh` from the web server job `w0788tM1wzXGHLzNaKKa`
(sources in `data/README.md`). We want to understand:

1. what the authors gave CausalCCC: the mosaic table, the variable list, the L-R pairs, the settings;
2. what CausalCCC returned;
3. whether the network supports what the paper says about Figure 3.

The new feature of this case study is that there are **three cell types**, and each one is both a sender and a
receiver. The table also contains **metadata** (cell subtype and skin condition) as extra variables.

This notebook only **reads** files: nothing in `data/` is modified and nothing is written.

## Setup

The helper functions used in notebooks 01 and 02 (`find_repo_root()`, `neighbors_of()`, `graph_distance()`, ...) are now
in `scripts/helpers.R`, so that every notebook uses the same version. We load them with `source()`.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)

# find_repo_root() is needed before we know where helpers.R is, so this short loop is repeated here
root <- getwd()
while (!file.exists(file.path(root, "scripts", "helpers.R"))) {
  if (dirname(root) == root) stop("Repository root not found. Open the repository folder in Positron.")
  root <- dirname(root)
}
source(file.path(root, "scripts", "helpers.R"))

job_dir <- file.path(root, "data", "case2", "causalccc_server_w0788tM1wzXGHLzNaKKa")
if (!dir.exists(job_dir)) stop("Data not found: run scripts/case2/download_case2.sh first.")
```

## 1. Read the files

The same files as in case study 1. `guess_max = Inf` tells `read_tsv()` to look at every row before deciding the type of
a column: the metadata columns are empty (`NA`) for thousands of rows before their first value, and without this option
they would be read as logical columns.

```{r}
#| label: read-files

mosaic      <- read_tsv(file.path(job_dir, "input.tsv"), guess_max = Inf, show_col_types = FALSE)
state_order <- read_tsv(file.path(job_dir, "clean_state_order.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
lr_pairs    <- read_tsv(file.path(job_dir, "clean_interact_edges.tsv"),
                        col_names = c("ligand", "receptor"), show_col_types = FALSE)
edges       <- read_tsv(file.path(job_dir, "edgesList.miic.summary.txt"), show_col_types = FALSE)
run_log     <- read_lines(file.path(job_dir, "whole_run.log"))

tibble(
  table   = c("mosaic", "state_order", "lr_pairs", "edges"),
  rows    = c(nrow(mosaic), nrow(state_order), nrow(lr_pairs), nrow(edges)),
  columns = c(ncol(mosaic), ncol(state_order), ncol(lr_pairs), ncol(edges))
)
```

The mosaic table is byte-for-byte identical to `data/case_study2/input.tsv`, the copy found online at the start of
the project (same md5 checksum, checked when downloading).

## 2. How the server ran

```{r}
#| label: run-command

run_log |>
  str_subset("^Rscript") |>
  str_replace_all(" (--?[a-z])", "\n  \\1") |>
  cat()
```

The settings are those of case study 1 (see notebook 02, section 2, for the meaning of each option), with one
exception: `--n_threads 1` instead of 2. The time stamps of the log give the running time on the server:

```{r}
#| label: run-time

run_log |>
  str_subset("START miic|Search for conditional|confidence cut|Done!") |>
  str_trunc(110) |>
  cat(sep = "\n")
```

About three hours, most of it spent searching for conditional independences. The confidence filter removed 72 links.

## 3. The mosaic table

Each row is a cell of one of the three types. The metadata columns `labels_<type>` (cell subtype) are filled only for
the cells of that type, so they tell us the type of each row. Then, as in notebook 01, the type of a column is the type
of the rows where it has values.

```{r}
#| label: rows-and-columns

cell_types <- c("Fibroblasts", "T_cell", "DCs")

row_type <- case_when(!is.na(mosaic$labels_Fibroblasts) ~ "Fibroblasts",
                      !is.na(mosaic$labels_T_cell)      ~ "T_cell",
                      !is.na(mosaic$labels_DCs)         ~ "DCs")

col_type <- column_cell_type(mosaic, row_type)

tibble(cell_type = cell_types,
       cells     = map_int(cell_types, \(t) sum(row_type == t, na.rm = TRUE)),
       variables = map_int(cell_types, \(t) sum(col_type == t)))

# Every row has a type, and every column belongs to exactly one type?
c(rows_without_type = sum(is.na(row_type)), columns_shared = sum(!col_type %in% cell_types))
```

Is the mosaic exactly made of three filled blocks? For each cell type we check that its rows are complete in its own
columns and empty everywhere else.

```{r}
#| label: check-blocks

map(cell_types, \(t) {
  own_rows <- row_type == t
  own_cols <- col_type == t
  tibble(cell_type          = t,
         own_block_complete = !anyNA(mosaic[own_rows, own_cols]),
         elsewhere_empty    = all(is.na(mosaic[own_rows, !own_cols])))
}) |> list_rbind()

rle(row_type)
```

Rows are grouped by cell type: dendritic cells, then T cells, then fibroblasts.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mosaic
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

col_order <- names(mosaic)[order(match(col_type, cell_types))]

mosaic |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(v) !is.na(v)), cell = row_number()) |>
  pivot_longer(-cell, names_to = "variable", values_to = "has_value") |>
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = col_order)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = variable, y = cell, fill = has_value)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "steelblue", `FALSE` = "grey90"),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "value", `FALSE` = "NA")) +
  labs(x = "variables (fibroblasts | T cells | dendritic cells)", y = "cells (rows of input.tsv)", fill = NULL,
       title = "The mosaic table uploaded to CausalCCC (case study 2)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```

### Variable names

In case study 1, a suffix (`_senders`, `_receivers`) was added only to genes measured on both sides. Here the rule
looks similar but has gone wrong in places: some names carry the suffix twice. We split each name into its gene and
its suffixes.

```{r}
#| label: names

names_tbl <- tibble(variable = names(mosaic), cell_type = col_type) |>
  mutate(suffixes = str_count(variable, paste0("_(", paste(cell_types, collapse = "|"), ")")),
         gene     = str_remove_all(variable, paste0("_(", paste(cell_types, collapse = "|"), ")")))

count(names_tbl, cell_type, suffixes)

names_tbl |> filter(suffixes == 2) |> pull(variable)
```

Once the suffixes are removed, does a gene appear twice in the same cell type? If so, we compare the two columns on the
cells of that type.

```{r}
#| label: duplicated-columns

duplicates <- names_tbl |>
  group_by(cell_type, gene) |>
  filter(n() == 2) |>
  summarise(copy_1 = first(variable), copy_2 = last(variable), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(identical = pmap_lgl(list(cell_type, copy_1, copy_2), \(t, a, b) {
    identical(mosaic[[a]][row_type == t], mosaic[[b]][row_type == t])
  }))

duplicates

# Any gene present more than twice in a cell type?
names_tbl |> count(cell_type, gene) |> filter(n > 2)
```

`r nrow(duplicates)` genes appear **twice in the same cell type, as two identical columns**. For example
`S100A6_Fibroblasts` and `S100A6_Fibroblasts_Fibroblasts` hold the same numbers, and so do `ACTB` and `ACTB_T_cell`. One
copy has one suffix more than the other. The table was probably assembled from several sender–receiver runs, in which
the same gene got different names (notebook 05, section 10). Section 7 shows what this does to the network.

### Variable types and groups

```{r}
#| label: state-order

count(state_order, group)

setequal(names(mosaic), state_order$var_names)

state_order |> filter(var_type == 0) |> select(var_names, levels_increasing_order)
```

The six discrete variables are the metadata: the cell subtype (`labels_*`, four subtypes per cell type, from the
CellChat annotation) and the skin condition (`condition_*`: `LS` lesional or `NL` non-lesional skin of atopic
dermatitis patients). Every gene is continuous.

```{r}
#| label: metadata

mosaic |>
  mutate(cell_type = row_type,
         subtype   = coalesce(labels_Fibroblasts, labels_T_cell, labels_DCs),
         condition = coalesce(condition_Fibroblasts, condition_T_cell, condition_DCs)) |>
  count(cell_type, condition) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = n)
```

Most dendritic cells and T cells come from lesional skin, while fibroblasts are more balanced.

### Raw counts?

```{r}
#| label: raw-counts

gene_cols <- state_order$var_names[state_order$var_type == 1]
values    <- unlist(mosaic[gene_cols], use.names = FALSE)
values    <- values[!is.na(values)]

tibble(minimum = min(values), maximum = max(values),
       all_integers = all(values == round(values)), fraction_zero = mean(values == 0))
```

## 4. The ligand–receptor pairs

The L-R pairs come from the CellChat analysis of this dataset (Jin *et al.*, *Nat Commun* 2021). Each ligand and
receptor name carries the cell type that expresses it, so we can read off the direction of each pair.

```{r}
#| label: lr-pairs

lr_pairs <- lr_pairs |>
  mutate(sender   = col_type[ligand],
         receiver = col_type[receptor])

count(lr_pairs, sender, receiver)

# Every ligand declared a ligand, every receptor a receptor?
lr_pairs |>
  summarise(all_ligands_ok   = all(ligand %in% state_order$var_names[state_order$group == "ligands"]),
            all_receptors_ok = all(receptor %in% state_order$var_names[state_order$group == "receptors"]))

lr_pairs |> filter(str_detect(ligand, "CXCL12"))
```

The pairs cover all six directions between two different cell types; there is no autocrine pair (ligand and receptor
in the same cell type). The pairs of Figure 3 (CXCL12 from fibroblasts to CXCR4 on dendritic cells and on T cells) are there.

How often is each ligand and receptor detected in its own cell type?

```{r}
#| label: lr-expression
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7

lr_genes <- unique(c(lr_pairs$ligand, lr_pairs$receptor))

lr_expression <- mosaic[lr_genes] |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "count") |>
  filter(!is.na(count)) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(fraction_detected = mean(count > 0)) |>
  mutate(role = if_else(variable %in% lr_pairs$ligand, "ligand", "receptor"))

ggplot(lr_expression, aes(x = fraction_detected, y = reorder(variable, fraction_detected), fill = role)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "cells of its own type where the gene is detected", y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       title = "Detection of ligands and receptors") +
  theme_minimal()

lr_expression |> filter(fraction_detected < 0.1) |> arrange(fraction_detected)
```

## 5. The published network

We sort the retained links into categories using the cell type of each variable.

```{r}
#| label: network

count(edges, type)

network <- edges |>
  filter(type == "P") |>
  mutate(type_x   = col_type[x],
         type_y   = col_type[y],
         category = if_else(type_x == type_y, paste("within", type_x), "ligand-receptor"))

count(network, category)

# Number of cells used to learn each kind of link
count(network, category, cells_used = Nxy_ai)
```

Links within a cell type are learnt from the cells of that type only; the 43 L-R links are given, not learnt
(`Nxy_ai` is `NA`).

```{r}
#| label: orientation

network |>
  mutate(orientation = case_when(infOrt ==  1 ~ "not oriented",
                                 infOrt %in% c(2, -2) ~ "oriented",
                                 infOrt ==  6 ~ "bidirected")) |>
  count(category, orientation) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = orientation, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

count(network, is_causal)
```

**Hubs.**

```{r}
#| label: hubs

bind_rows(select(network, gene = x), select(network, gene = y)) |>
  count(gene, name = "links", sort = TRUE) |>
  head(10)
```

**The metadata variables** are part of the network. Their neighbours show which genes differ between subtypes or
between lesional and non-lesional skin.

```{r}
#| label: metadata-links

metadata_vars <- state_order$var_names[state_order$group == "metadata"]

map(metadata_vars, \(m) neighbors_of(m, network)) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  group_by(node) |>
  summarise(links = n(), neighbors = paste(head(neighbor, 8), collapse = ", "))
```

## 6. Does the network support the paper's description of Figure 3?

Figure 3C shows the "second-degree neighbourhood" of the two CXCL12–CXCR4 links: the genes at most two links away from
CXCL12 in fibroblasts and from CXCR4 in dendritic cells and in T cells. The text names specific genes in that
neighbourhood. We look for them in the network **within each cell type**, that is, without the L-R links, which
would otherwise connect everything through the receptors.

```{r}
#| label: intracellular

intracellular <- network |> filter(category != "ligand-receptor")
```

**Statement 1.** CXCL12, secreted by fibroblasts, is linked to CXCR4 on dendritic cells and on T cells.

```{r}
#| label: claim-1

network |>
  filter(str_detect(x, "^CXCL12") | str_detect(y, "^CXCL12")) |>
  filter(category == "ligand-receptor") |>
  select(x, y, infOrt, proba)
```

**Statement 2.** Upstream of CXCL12 in fibroblasts: the fibroblast marker DCN and the adipose-related genes APOD and CFD.

```{r}
#| label: claim-2

neighbors_of("CXCL12_Fibroblasts", intracellular)

distance_cxcl12 <- graph_distance(intracellular, "CXCL12_Fibroblasts")
tibble(gene = c("DCN", "APOD", "CFD"), distance_from_CXCL12 = distance_cxcl12[gene])
```

**Statement 3.** Downstream of CXCR4 in dendritic cells: GPR183 (migration), NR4A3 and VIM. In the table VIM of
dendritic cells is called `VIM_DCs_DCs` (double suffix, section 3).

```{r}
#| label: claim-3

neighbors_of("CXCR4_DCs", intracellular)

distance_cxcr4_dc <- graph_distance(intracellular, "CXCR4_DCs")
tibble(gene = c("GPR183", "NR4A3", "VIM_DCs_DCs"), distance_from_CXCR4 = distance_cxcr4_dc[gene])
```

**Statement 4.** Downstream of CXCR4 in T cells: the AP-1 genes FOS and JUNB.

```{r}
#| label: claim-4

neighbors_of("CXCR4_T_cell", intracellular)

distance_cxcr4_t <- graph_distance(intracellular, "CXCR4_T_cell")
tibble(gene = c("FOS", "JUNB"), distance_from_CXCR4 = distance_cxcr4_t[gene])
```

**The whole second-degree neighbourhood** (to compare by eye with Figure 3C):

```{r}
#| label: neighbourhood

second_degree <- function(from) {
  d <- graph_distance(intracellular, from)
  d <- d[d <= 2]
  tibble(centre = from, gene = names(d), distance = d)
}

map(c("CXCL12_Fibroblasts", "CXCR4_DCs", "CXCR4_T_cell"), second_degree) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  filter(distance > 0) |>
  group_by(centre, distance) |>
  summarise(genes = paste(sort(gene), collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop")
```

**Figure 3B** shows CXCL12 and CXCR4 expression in lesional skin. We draw the equivalent from the raw counts of the
mosaic (on a `log1p` scale, i.e. log(1 + count)), separating lesional and non-lesional cells.

```{r}
#| label: fig-3b
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4

tibble(cell_type = row_type,
       condition = coalesce(mosaic$condition_Fibroblasts, mosaic$condition_T_cell, mosaic$condition_DCs),
       CXCL12    = mosaic$CXCL12_Fibroblasts,
       CXCR4     = coalesce(mosaic$CXCR4_DCs, mosaic$CXCR4_T_cell)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(CXCL12, CXCR4), names_to = "gene", values_to = "count") |>
  filter(!is.na(count)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = cell_type, y = log1p(count), fill = condition)) +
  geom_violin(scale = "width") +
  facet_wrap(~gene, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log(1 + raw count)", fill = "skin",
       title = "CXCL12 in fibroblasts, CXCR4 in dendritic cells and T cells") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 7. What do the duplicated columns do to the network?

Two identical columns carry the same information, so MIIC finds the strongest possible link between them.

```{r}
#| label: duplicate-links

duplicate_links <- link_name(duplicates$copy_1, duplicates$copy_2)

# Are the two copies of each duplicated gene linked to each other?
edges |>
  filter(link_name(x, y) %in% duplicate_links) |>
  count(type)

network |>
  filter(link_name(x, y) %in% duplicate_links) |>
  select(x, y, info_shifted, partial_correlation)

# Rank of the strongest links among gene-gene links
network |>
  filter(category != "ligand-receptor") |>
  arrange(desc(info_shifted)) |>
  select(x, y, info_shifted) |>
  head(8)
```

The 14 links between copies are the 14 strongest gene–gene links of their cell types, with a partial correlation of
exactly 1. Since the L-R links are given the strength of the strongest link of the network, a duplicate also sets the
strength of every L-R link.

Do the two copies of a gene have the same neighbours (apart from each other)?

```{r}
#| label: duplicate-neighbours

intracellular_all <- network |> filter(category != "ligand-receptor")

duplicates |>
  mutate(neighbours = map2(copy_1, copy_2, \(a, b) {
    n_a <- setdiff(neighbors_of(a, intracellular_all)$neighbor, b)
    n_b <- setdiff(neighbors_of(b, intracellular_all)$neighbor, a)
    tibble(links_copy_1 = length(n_a), links_copy_2 = length(n_b), shared = length(intersect(n_a, n_b)))
  })) |>
  unnest(neighbours) |>
  select(cell_type, gene, links_copy_1, links_copy_2, shared)
```

Each duplicated gene thus enters the network twice, with each neighbour linked to both copies: its links are counted
twice, which inflates its importance as a hub. The two copies also count as two variables when MIIC looks for
separating sets and for orientations. For the Figure 3 claims this matters little (none of the genes named in the text
is duplicated), but it should be fixed when we rebuild the input.

## What we learned

**Inputs.** The mosaic has 7,563 cells (4,734 fibroblasts, 2,200 T cells, 629 dendritic cells): the full CellChat
`data_humanSkin` dataset, i.e. all cells of these three types from He *et al.* 2020. It has 238 variables: 232 genes
(raw integer counts) and 6 discrete metadata (cell subtype and lesional/non-lesional skin, for each cell type). The
43 CellChat L-R pairs connect the three cell types in both directions.

**Network.** 715 links were kept out of 8,458 examined. The server needed about three hours, single-threaded.

**Paper's statements (Figure 3C).** All supported, within the second-degree neighbourhood that the figure draws:

- CXCL12 in fibroblasts is linked to CXCR4 in dendritic cells and in T cells (given L-R links).
- CFD is a direct neighbour of CXCL12; DCN and APOD are two links away. Note that MIIC orients the link CXCL12 → CFD
  (not a genuine causation): CFD is on the fibroblast side, but the network does not put it upstream of CXCL12.
- NR4A3 is a direct neighbour of CXCR4 in dendritic cells; GPR183 and VIM are two links away.
- JUNB is a direct neighbour of CXCR4 in T cells; FOS is two links away.

The paper speaks of "upstream" and "downstream" genes. None of the links around CXCR4 is oriented, and the only
oriented links of CXCL12 point away from it, so these words describe the position relative to the L-R link (sender side,
receiver side) rather than a causal direction found by MIIC.

**Points for the preprocessing assessment.**

- 14 genes appear twice in the same cell type as identical columns, under two names that differ by one suffix
  (`S100A6_Fibroblasts` / `S100A6_Fibroblasts_Fibroblasts`, `ACTB` / `ACTB_T_cell`, ...). The link between two copies
  is the strongest of its cell type, and the gene's links are counted twice (section 7).
- Two L-R genes are detected in fewer than 10 % of the cells of their type: CCL19 (6 % of fibroblasts) and CD74 in
  fibroblasts (8 %).
- Dendritic cells are few (629) and mostly from lesional skin: links within dendritic cells are learnt from fewer cells.
